ChIJk1G1VInnOkcRXNdUd5Xk-00.4b86341b6176:
The comment from Kaazaam G2 matches our experience exactly. If you're considering working with Focusweb, read this short story so you don't get burned. And if Focusweb has their own take on the conflict, I'm perfectly willing to attach screenshots of our conversations so you can see everything with your own eyes.

Honestly, it's been six months already. But recently we had to completely redo the site because it was barely functional. That brought back all the nerves and time we'd wasted, and I felt compelled to warn others so no one repeats our sad experience.

Design.
We had our own design, yet we were politely but very persistently pressured to adopt something of theirs. Worth noting: a designer does design work, a programmer does programming. At Focusweb, the design competency is highly questionable — starting with the very basics of composition. Not surprising — programmers shouldn't be doing design. And yet the programmers constantly interfered and insisted, even after we'd repeated five times that we wanted to stick to the mockup.

Deviations from the mockup.
In the end we got a mountain of discrepancies from the mockup: alignment on the wrong side, wrong font sizes. To get each individual issue fixed, we had to call dozens of times. We hired a professional designer so everything would be done properly and precisely, not by eye. We paid for that. And Focusweb botched it all because, in their subjective opinion, it looks fine as is.

Revisions.
The revisions phase was the most painful part. I'm afraid to say exactly how long it lasted — six months or almost a year. It goes like this:
- I put together lists of about 10 items, with descriptions of the issues and accompanying screenshots
- the manager replies mostly in vague generalities, saying she'll find out how long it will take and let me know (something along those lines)
- from Friday to Friday I call the manager, and every time I'm promised "by the end of next week"
- eventually I call Kyrylo, as the head of the company, and ask him to sort things out. It's hard to be angry at Kyrylo, unlike the manager, who speaks to clients in a rather unpleasant manner. Kyrylo manipulates with his politeness, since he too fails to deliver on promises on time, just like his managers.
- when all the fixes are finally ready after a month or two, problems crop up somewhere else on the site. The cycle starts over
- on top of everything, they regularly try to convince me that the site isn't broken — I just have a browser problem. When I clear the cache and also check the site from 4 other computers, I finally force the manager to log into my computer via TeamViewer. Only then does it turn out the problem is fixed in 20 minutes.

Mobile version.
As agreed, the mobile version was included in the price. They promised to adapt the mockup to gadget dimensions. In practice they simply cropped the mockup left and right, causing us to lose 2/3 of the images. On the remaining points the mobile version is also practically unusable. Too bad I no longer have the screenshots so you could see this circus with your own eyes.

Extra charges.
Both for the mobile version and for countless other fixes, they tried to squeeze more money out of us. For some items you could at least argue, but mostly it involved things that had been agreed upon upfront. On top of that, without many of those fixes the site simply didn't function properly at all.
An important point: the amounts they asked for extra payment were so obviously absurd that no client would ever pay them. I suspect this means the company simply didn't have a specialist capable of handling the tasks at hand. So Focusweb tried to frame things in a way that would make the client walk away on their own.

Manager Yuliia.
I want to say something specific about Yuliia — the woman they put in charge of answering all my questions. What exactly was Yuliia's job, when every time I called, the answer started with Yuliia saying she's not handling this issue, she needs to check with so-and-so. The whole point of a manager, I thought, is to coordinate everyone's work and be able to give the client a status update. Perpetually confused, frightened, clueless Yuliia couldn't competently answer a single one of my questions — like a secretary asked to watch the phone while the actual manager went to lunch. When I finally managed to get her replaced, things moved forward just a little.

A review of IT Academy in Dnipro, regarding a paid course. In August I started a paid HTML/CSS/JavaScript course. It cost 6000 UAH.
You could find the same course online for 1500 UAH or even less.

In-person lectures and daily instructor support were advertised. The instructor not only failed to provide the promised support even once, but also behaved unprofessionally: didn't answer calls, cancelled promised meetings, would schedule meetings and then ask you to wait 40 minutes outside the door, scheduled meetings in a different location and cancelled them on the same day.

The promised mentorship from the instructor never materialized, despite my repeated requests.

During the course I tried calling the number listed on the IT Academy page to do something about the situation. I was told there was simply no administrator available to discuss the issue and was advised to write a letter to HR.

After my letter to HR, the course instructor personally reached out to me and, via SMS and email, stated she was ready to refund the full cost of the course — even though in my letter I had only asked for a partial refund for the promised support that was never delivered.

However, the academy director told me that a refund is a complicated procedure and refused to issue one, instead offering additional hours with a different instructor.

If the Academy had more organization and less chaos, I would have more trust and would have gladly taken those hours.

But after all the wasted nerves and time, the ethical thing for the academy would have been to compensate with a refund, since the course content itself may also be of poor quality.

If I had known there would be no support, I would have taken an equivalent course online for a quarter of the price.

I also want to note that the call center in Lviv was often rude, and they didn't contact me for 2 weeks after I signed up for the course, which made me worried and start looking at alternatives. They explained the delay by a corporate event that apparently took place in July.

The instructor also cited a company trip to a holiday event in Kyiv as the reason she couldn't hold a promised class.
